¶
'''Young-Helmholtz theory of color.''' See ''color.''

'''youngling''' (yung′ling), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ME. ''yongling'', ''ȝongling'', ''ȝungling'', < AS. ''geongling'' (= OHG. ''jungeling''), a young man, < ''geong'', young, + ''-ling'', E. ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A young person; a youth or child.
{{smaller block|<poem>Due privilege allow’d, we all should go
Before, and she, the ''youngling'', come behind.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, iv. 10.}}}}
'''2.''' Any young thing, as an animal, a plant, etc.; anything immature, undeveloped, or recent.
{{smaller block|More dear unto their God then ''younglings'' to their dam.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. x. 57.}}
<poem>Speak, whimp’ring ''younglings'', and make known
The reason why
Ye droop and weep.</poem>
{{right|''Herrick'', To Primroses Fill’d with Morning Dew.}}}}
'''3.''' A novice; a new-comer; a beginner.
{{smaller block|This Naaman was but an ''youngling'' in God’s religion.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Works (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 338.}}}}
'''II.''' ''a.'' Youthful; young.
{{smaller block|<poem>The mountain raven’s ''youngling'' brood
Have left the mother and the nest.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Idle Shepherd-boys.}}
The frequent chequer of a ''youngling'' tree.
{{right|''Keats'', I Stood Tiptoe upon a Little Hill.}}}}

'''youngly''' (yung′li), ''a.'' [< ME. ''ȝongly'', ''ȝunglich'', < AS. ''geonglic'', < ''geong'', young, + ''-līc'', E. ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Youthful.
{{smaller block|Sum men clepen it the Welle of Zouthe: for thei that often drynken there of semen alle weys ''Ȝongly'', and lyven with outen Sykenesse. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 169.}}}}
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''youngly''' (yung′li), ''adv.'' [< ''young'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In youth; as a youth.
{{smaller block|How ''youngly'' he began to serve his country.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 3. 244.}}}}

'''youngness''' (yung′nes), ''n.'' [< ''young'' + ''-ness.''] The condition of being young. ''Cudworth.''

'''Young’s modulus.''' See ''modulus.''

'''youngster''' (yung′stėr), ''n.'' [< ''young'' + ''-ster.''] '''1.''' A young person; a lad: sometimes applied also to young animals, especially horses.
{{smaller block|For Adon’s sake, a ''youngster'' proud and wild.
{{right|''Shak.'', Passionate Pilgrim, l. 120.}}
A ''youngster'' at school, more sedate than the rest.
{{right|''Cowper'', Pity for Poor Africans.}}
With the exception of her full sister, . . . this filly is considered the highest bred trotting ''youngster'' now on the American continent.
{{right|''New York Evening Post'', June 28, 1889.}}}}
'''2.''' A junior officer in a company, battery, or troop. [Familiar and colloq.]

'''youngth†''' (yungth), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''yongth''; < ME. ''yongth, ȝongthe, ȝungthe''; < ''young'' + ''-th''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''youth'', an older word of the same ult. elements.] Youth.
{{smaller block|The lusty ''yongth'' of mans might.
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant. (ed. 1554), p. clxviii.}}
The mornefull Muse in myrth now list ne maske,
As shee was wont in ''youngth'' and sommer dayes.
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., November.}}}}

'''youngthly†''' (yungth′li), ''a.'' [Formerly ''yongthly''; < ''youngth'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Youthful.
{{smaller block|<poem>He breathlesse did remaine,
And all his ''yongthly'' forces idly spent.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Muiopotmos, l. 431.}}}}

And., iv. 3. 91.}}}} {{smaller block|King Edward the sixt, being of ''young'' yeres, but olde in wit. {{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 158.}}}} '''7.''' Junior: applied to the younger of two persons, especially when they have the same name or title: as, ''young'' Mr. Thomas Ray called with a message from his father. [Colloq.] —'''8.''' Newly or lately arrived. [Australia.] {{smaller block|So says I, “You’re rather ''young'' there, a’n’t you? I was by there a fortnight ago.” {{right|''H. Kingsley'', Geoffry Hamlyn, p. 33.}}}} {{smaller|'''The Young Pretender.''' See ''pretender'', 3.—'''Young America,''' the rising generation in the United States. [Colloq.]—'''Young beer.''' See ''schenk beer'', under ''beer''1.—'''Young blood.''' See ''blood''.—'''Young England,''' a group of Tory politicians, chiefly recruited from the younger members of the aristocracy, who, about 1844, opposed free trade and radicalism, and advocated the restoration of the supposed former condition of things. Among their leaders were Disraeli and Lord John Manners.—'''Young flood, fustic, hyson, ice.''' See the nouns.—'''Young Ireland,''' a group of Irish politicians and agitators, active about 1840–50, who were at first adherents of O’Connell, but were separated from him through their advocacy of physical force, and took part in the rising of 1848.—'''Young Italy,''' an association of Italian republican agitators, active about 1834, under the lead of Mazzini. Analogous republican groups in other countries were called ''Young Germany'', ''Young Poland'', and ''Young France'', and these republican associations collectively were known as ''Young Europe''.}} '''II.''' ''n.'' Offspring collectively. The egg that soon Bursting with kindly rupture forth disclosed Their callow ''young''. {{smaller block|{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vii. 420.}}}} The mother-linnet in the brake Bewails her ravish’d ''young''. {{smaller block|{{right|''Burns'', A Mother’s Lament.}}}} '''With young''', pregnant; gravid. {{smaller block|So many days my ewes have been ''with young''. {{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 5. 35.}}}} '''Young of the year''', in ''ornith.'', specifically, birds which have left the nest and acquired their first plumage. Most birds hatch in summer, and, after putting off the down-feathers characteristic of the nestling, acquire a special first feathering; and as long as this is worn, or until the first true molt, they are ''young of the year'', without regard to the length of time this plumage may be worn, as it is always replaced by the following spring. Dan. ''junker''); < MD. ''joncker'', D. ''jonker'' = MLG. ''junker'', ''juncher'', LG. ''junker'' = MHG. ''junker'', ''junkher'', ''junckher'', ''jonker'', G. ''junker'', a young gentleman, a young man; contracted and reduced to the form of a derivative in ''-er'', < D. ''jonkheer'' = LG. ''jungheer'' = MHG. ''junchērre'', ''juncherre'', G. ''jungherr'', ''junger Herr'', young gentleman: see ''young'' and ''herre''1, ''herr''. Cf. G. ''jungfer'', similarly reduced from ''jungfrau''.]   '''1†.''' A young man of condition; a young gentleman or knight. {{smaller block|Amongst the rest, there was a jolly knight; . . . But that same ''younker'' soone was overthrowne. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. i. 11.}}}} {{smaller block|Ulysses slept there, and close by The other ''younkers''. {{right|''Chapman'', Odyssey, xiv.}}}} '''2.''' A young person; a lad; a youngster. {{smaller block|Pagget, a school-boy, got a sword, and then He vow’d destruction both to birch and men; Who wo’d not think this ''yonker'' fierce to fight? {{right|''Herrick'', Upon Pagget.}}}} {{smaller block|It was a pleasure to see the sable ''younkers'' lick in the unctuous meat. {{right|''Lamb'', Chimney-Sweepers.}}}} {{smaller block|The juveniles and ''younkers'' in the town. {{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 6.}}}} '''3†.''' A novice; a simpleton; a dupe. {{smaller block|What, will you make a ''younker'' of me? shall I not take mine ease in mine inn but I shall have my pocket picked? {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iii. 3. 92.}}}} {{smaller block|''Ang.'' Is he your brother, sir? ''Eust.'' Yes.—Would he were buried! I fear he’ll make an ass of me, a ''younker''. {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Elder Brother, iii. 5.}}}} '''4.''' Same as ''junker''. '''youpon''' (yö′pọn), ''n.'' Same as ''yapon.'' '''your''' (yör), ''pron.''   [(''a'') < ME. ''your, ȝour, ȝoure, ȝure, iour, eower,'' < AS. ''eówer'' (= OS. ''iuwar'' = OHG. ''iuwer'' = Goth. ''izwara''), gen. of ''gē'' (dat. acc. ''eów''), you: see ''ye''1, ''you.'' (''b'') < ME. ''your, ȝour, ȝoure, ȝowre, iour, ower, our, eoure, eowre, eower,'' < AS. ''eówer'' = OS. ''iuwar, iuwa'' = OFries. ''iuwe,'' etc., = Goth. ''izwar,'' poss. pron.: see (''a''), above.]   '''A†.''' ''pers. pron.'' Of you: the original genitive of ''ye''1, ''you.'' {{smaller block|Sitthen I am ''ȝoure'' alre hefd [i. e., head of you all],
ich am ''ȝoure'' alre hele [salvation]. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxii. 473.}}}} '''B.''' ''poss. pron.'' '''1†.''' Of you; belonging to you: used predicatively: now replaced by ''yours.'' {{smaller block|I wolde permute [change] my penaunce with ''ȝowre.'' {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xiii. 110.}}}} {{smaller block|I . . . mot ben ''youre'' whil that my lyf may dure. {{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 642.}}}} {{smaller block|And she ansuerde, “I am ''youre'' and the childe ''youre'', therfore do with me and with hym youre will.” {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 89.}}}} '''2.''' Belonging to you: possessive and adjective in use, preceding the noun. {{smaller|While plural in form and original meaning, it is now commonly also used, like the nominative ''you'', in addressing an individual.}} {{smaller block|“I haue no kynde knowyng,” quod I, “to conceyue alle ''ȝoure'' wordes.” {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), viii. 57.}}}} {{smaller block|Promise unto the Lord ''your'' God, and keep it, all ye that are round about him. {{right|''Book of Common Prayer'', Psalter, Ps. lxxvi. 11.}}}} {{smaller block|I leave it [the poem] to ''your'' honourable survey, and ''your'' honour to ''your'' heart’s content. {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, Ded. to the Earl of Southampton.}}}} {{smaller block|[''Your'' was used formerly to denote a class or species well known. This use survives as an archaism, and now often adds a slurring or humorous significance. ''Your'' serpent of Egypt is bred now of ''your'' mud by the operation of ''your'' sun. {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 7. 29.}}}} {{smaller block|''Your'' great Philosophers have been voluntarily poor. {{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 352.]}}}} '''yourn''' (yörn), ''pron.'' Yours.   [Prov. Eng. and U. S.] '''yours''' (yörz), ''pron.''   [< ME. ''youres'', ''ȝoures'', etc.; with added poss. suffix, as in ''ours'', ''theirs'', etc.: see ''your''.]   That which belongs or those which belong to you: the possessive used without a following noun. {{smaller|Preceded by ''of'', it is equivalent to the personal pronoun ''you'': as, a friend ''of yours''. Compare the similar phrases made with the other possessives in the independent form.}} {{smaller block|Ye cruell one! what glory can be got In slaying him that would live gladly ''yours!'' {{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, lvii.}}}} {{smaller block|What’s mine is ''yours'' and what is ''yours'' is mine. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 543.}}}} {{smaller block|''Yours'' is no love, Faith and Religion fly it. {{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|If by Fate ''yours'' only must be Empire, then of necessitie ours among the rest must be subjection. {{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|[''Yours'' is sometimes used in specific senses without reference to a noun previously mentioned: (''a'') Your property. (''b'') The persons belonging to you; your friends or relatives. Bothe to me & to myne mykull vnright, And to yow & also ''yours'' ȝomeryng [mourning] for euer. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1722.}}}} {{smaller block|O God, I fear thy justice will take hold On me, and you, and mine, and ''yours'' for this! {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 1. 132.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') Your letter: as, ''yours'' of the 16th inst. is at hand.}} {{smaller block|I have ''yours'' just now of the 19th. {{right|''Swift'', To Dr. Sheridan, July 27, 1726.]}}}} Abbreviated ''yrs.'' '''Yours truly, yours to command''', etc., {{smaller|phrases of conventional politeness immediately preceding the signature at the end of a letter: hence sometimes used playfully by a speaker in alluding to himself.}} {{smaller block|''Yours truly'', sir, has an eye for a fine woman and a fine horse. {{right|''W. Collins'', Armadale, II. 168. (''Hoppe.'')}}}} '''yourself, yourselves''' (yör-self′, -selvz′), ''pron.''   [< ME. ''your selven'', etc.: see ''your'' and ''self''.]   An emphatic or reflexive form of the second personal pronoun, ''ye, you.'' {{smaller|''Yourself'' is used when a single person is addressed (compare ''ye, your''), and ''yourselves'' when more than one. As nominatives, the words are used for emphasis, either in apposition with ''you'' or alone.}} {{smaller block|Ye se well ''your-seluyn'' the sothe at your egh, Hit is no bote here to byde for baret with-oute. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 12333.}}}} {{smaller block|I knowe yow alle as wele or beter than ye do ''youre-self.'' {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 141.}}}} {{smaller block|Conversation is but carving; Carve for all, ''yourself'' is starving. {{right|''Swift'', Verses on a Lady.}}}} {{smaller|In the objective case ''yourself'' or ''yourselves'' is commonly reflexive: when emphatic it is usually in apposition with ''you.'' Compare ''himself, herself'', etc.}} {{smaller block|Call forth your actors by the scroll. Masters, spread ''yourselves.'' {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 2. 16.}}}} “Stay then a little,” answered Julian, “here, And keep ''yourself'', none knowing, to ''yourself''.” {{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Lover’s Tale, Golden Supper.}}}} '''yourta, yourte,''' ''n.'' French spellings of ''yurt.'' '''youse''' (yöz), ''n.''   [E. Ind.]   The chetah or hunting-leopard, ''Guepardus jubatus.'' Also ''youze.'' See cut under ''chetah.'' '''youth''' (yöth), ''n.''   [< ME. ''youthe, youhthe, iouthe, ȝouthe, yhouthe, ȝuwethe, ȝuȝethe, ȝeoȝuthe, iuȝethe,'' etc., < AS. ''geógoth, gióguth, iugoth'' = OS. ''juguth, jugud'' = D. ''jeugd'' = OHG. ''jugund,'' MHG. ''jugent,'' G. ''jugend,'' youth; with abstract formative ''-th'' (''-oth,'' etc.), < AS. ''geong,'' etc., young: see ''young.'' A “restored” form appears in ''youngth.'']   '''1.''' The condition of being young; youthfulness; youngness; juvenility. {{smaller block|These opinions have ''youth'' in their countenance; antiquity knew them not; it never thought nor dreamed of them. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, vi. 4.}}}} In fact, there ’s nothing that keeps its ''youth'', So far as I know, but a tree and truth. {{smaller block|{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', The Deacon’s Masterpiece.}}}} '''2.''' The age from puberty up to the attainment of full growth. {{smaller|In a general sense, youth denotes the whole early part of life, from infancy to maturity; but it is not unusual to divide the stages of life into infancy, childhood, youth, and manhood. Thus limited, youth includes that early period of manhood or womanhood upon which one enters at puberty, with the establishment of the sexual functions, and in which one continues until the skeleton is completely ossified by the consolidation of the epiphyses of the long bones, so that there is no further increase in stature, and all the teeth are in permanent functional position.}}
